chapter_theme: Civakan answers his mother, travels with his company through forest to a river country, is feasted, sung to and loved at a grove halt, worships the Jina at dawn, and enters the city, where the women cannot tell him from Murugan or Kama and a maiden is playing ball.

cast.role: the hero, travelling to the city where Vimalai lives
Civakan's mother, whose counsel he answers in 1932
the young men of Civakan's company
the women who cook, serve and sing for Civakan at the halt
the women of the city who throng to see Civakan
the maiden playing ball, not named in these verses

1932.reading: Civakan accepts his mother's counsel: he will go next day to that city, show his own people the truth, and come back the same day, and he asks her to go ahead to the one of the victorious elephant.
1932.nuance: அடிகள் is his address to his mother; the one of the victorious elephant (வென்றிக் களிற்றுன்) is most likely the maternal uncle (மாமன்) she named in 1931, but the verse does not name him.
1932.event: Civakan tells Vijayai he will go to the city to show his kin the truth and asks her to go to her brother.

1933.reading: The young man of the strong bow set out toward the forest hot as spear-points, walking with his band, his road guarded by riders on wind-swift horses and an army fit for the journey.
1933.nuance: நூற்றைவர் gives the size of his band, a hundred and five or five hundred depending on how the compound is read.
1933.event: Civakan sets out through the hot forest with his company and a guard of horsemen.

1934.reading: Crossing hills where falls never cease and rivers ringed with cool tanks, the hero of the gem-mountain chest reached a river country of fields and groves.
1934.event: Civakan reaches a fertile river country.

1935.reading: The scent of flowers opening on the groves, the breath of lotuses in the pools and the sandal the women wore met the newcomer at every turn as feast after feast.
1935.nuance: The land itself plays host: the fragrances are said to make விருந்து, the guest's welcome, before any person greets him.

1936.reading: He of the gold-wrought gem ornaments halted in a divine flower grove where bees, drunk on honey dripping from comb into lotuses, hummed like a tuned yaazh.
1936.event: Civakan halts in a flowering grove.

1937.reading: The pack beasts were unloaded, the young men of gem anklets were rid of their weariness, and the women of fragrant garlands made the four kinds of food of six tastes for the lord of the famed spear.
1937.event: The company rests and the women prepare a meal for Civakan.

1938.reading: Nosebags were filled with jaggery rice, boiled pulse and horse-gram for the horses, while the other beasts grazed tall cane and red paddy, drank, and rested in the rich shade.
1938.event: The horses and other beasts are fed and rested.

1939.reading: Only after the man like a musth elephant had eaten the sweet food served by the women with dripping garlands did the backwater lotuses, open like eyes, close for the evening.
1939.nuance: The closing of the lotuses waits on his meal, so evening is timed to the guest.
1939.event: Civakan eats the meal the women serve as evening falls.

1940.reading: Gem lamps glimmered, sweet smoke rose, strings sounded, flutes sang, and the drum and gold cymbals made a pleasant din.

1941.reading: After the women of red mouths and rain-dark fish eyes had kindled desire with songs sweeter than nectar, he went to the soft bed.
1941.nuance: வேனலான் அளித்த பின் in line 3 is hard to place: it may name the spring god Kama as the giver, or a song of the hot season.
1941.event: The women sing to Civakan and he retires to bed.

1942.reading: Shoulders strong enough to crush sweet cane and swelling lovely shoulders entwined, hot breasts pressed against his cool garland till its gold dust fell, and so he swam across the dark night.
1942.nuance: The verse does not name his partner; the context of 1941 makes it the singing women. The Jain epic tells the hero's night of pleasure without a word of reproach and moves straight to his dawn worship of the Jina.
1942.event: Civakan spends the night in love.

1943.reading: When the sun opened its eye at dawn, the hero like Murugan washed his radiant face with a hand like a budding lotus, showered flowers and bowed to the Lord (முனைவன்).
1943.nuance: முனைவன் is the Jain name for the Jina; the morning rite follows the night of 1942 with no sense of conflict between them.
1943.event: At dawn Civakan washes and worships the Lord.

1944.reading: His daily duties done, the hero of the famed spear went quickly, in a form that bangled women desire, to see the wealth of the sword-guarded city.
1944.event: Civakan goes into the city to see its riches.

1945.reading: The long city's wealth never runs short: lac paste slipping from feet, ornaments cast off in lovers' sulks, golden petals strewn by garlands that trail along the ground.
1945.nuance: The wealth is proved by what is wasted: ornaments thrown off in புலத்தல், the lovers' quarrel, lie in the street as litter.

1946.reading: The sandal-painted breasts of the women whose garlands smell of the kazhuneer lily turn even those whose minds run toward release (சித்தி) back in this direction.
1946.nuance: சித்தி here is the final attainment of the Jain path, not yogic power; the verse is praise of the city's women, and the seekers' lapse is its measure.

1947.reading: Within the circle of the walls there is no room for anything but crowds of women whose waists shame the vanji creeper, with dyed feet and anklets, and young men in crowned locks.

1948.reading: The women like golden creepers lament: is he the tall Vel of the long kadamba, or the son of the five arrows and the long bow? We cannot tell; tell us.
1948.event: The city's women, seeing Civakan, cry out that they cannot tell whether he is Murugan or Kama.

1949.reading: His true form, like a youth of the heavens, seizes and devours all the long eyes of the women, as a bird of the backwater takes fish.
1949.nuance: The usual figure is reversed: elsewhere women's eyes are the fish or the arrows; here his beauty is the bird that eats their eyes.

1950.reading: Maidens crowded upon the man of the flesh-tipped spear, holding up garlands with gem strands, their breasts thrusting, as if they would drink him with their eyes.
1950.event: Young women crowd round Civakan with garlands.

1951.reading: While the women everywhere aim their eye-arrows at the young man in the street, a girl like a daughter of the gods, with eyes like a doe's and speech sweet as milk, is playing ball.
1951.nuance: The girl is not named here; the ilampakam's title makes her Vimalai. She is absorbed in her game while every other woman is looking at him.
1951.event: A maiden is playing ball in the street where Civakan walks.

1952.reading: Her garland bounces, her hot breasts and pearl strings shift, her gem earrings swing like bows, her gold ear-leaf flashes, and her girdle and anklets ring as she dances at the ball.
1952.nuance: The verse changes to a quick சந்தம் rhythm that moves with the ball.

links.note: The patikam promised that Civakan would enter the city's sky-high streets and fall into the sea of nectar of a maiden born by a boon; 1951 brings him into the street and shows her at her ball.
links.teaches: The patikam's figure of him falling into her sea of nectar is set up with a reversal: in the street it is the other women who shoot their eyes at him, while the destined maiden is first seen paying him no attention at all.

links.note: Routed kings cried that Civakan was Murugan on his peacock; the city's women now ask whether he is Murugan or Kama.
links.teaches: The likeness to Murugan that the defeated kings shouted in terror returns as a question of desire in the women's mouths, so one image carries both his name in war and his effect in the street.

links.note: Kural 1081's man cannot tell whether the woman is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; here the women cannot tell whether the man is Murugan or Kama.
links.teaches: The epic gives the first-sight bewilderment of the Kural's lover to a crowd of women looking at a man, and narrows the choice to two gods, so the doubt is no longer whether the beloved is mortal but which divine lover he is.

gains.a: the epic verse gains a recognised convention, the lover's dazed question at first sight, which marks the women's cry as love struck at a glance rather than plain praise
gains.b: the couplet gains a case with a plural female speaker, showing its doubt is a form of first sight that the tradition could turn round, not something tied to the man's voice

links.note: The epic praises the city's women for drawing back even minds bent on release; the Siddhar reproaches his heart for sinking into lust for women after keeping the company of ascetics.
links.teaches: The same lapse, a seeker of release pulled back by women, is the epic's yardstick of beauty and the Siddhar's confession of madness, so what one poet spends as a compliment is the very failure the other's renunciation is built to fight.

gains.a: the epic's hyperbole gains the view of the seeker it uses as a measure, for whom being drawn back is ruin and not a tribute to anyone's beauty
gains.b: the Siddhar's self-reproach gains the voice of the world he turns from, where the same pull is celebrated as a city's glory, so his struggle is against a culture's praise as well as his own heart

source_issues: 1950 and 1951 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
1932 line 2 (எமர்க்கேயேன துண்மை) has a doubtful word division; the sense 'show the truth to our people' is clear, the verb is not.
1933 line 2 நூற்றைவர் can be read as a hundred and five or five hundred.
1952 line 2 (நிழன்மலிந்த நோவடந்நி ழற்படப்ப டைத்தர) is broken by the printed division and hard to construe.
